items.stem: What is the name for "the decomposition of a compound, molten or in aqueous solution, by passing an electric current through it"?
items.answer: Electrolysis
items.markingKey: Electrolysis: the decomposition of a compound, molten or in aqueous solution, by passing an electric current through it.

items.stem: Explain why twice as much charge is needed to deposit one mole of copper as one mole of silver.
items.answer: Copper is deposited from Cu²⁺, which needs 2 electrons per atom; silver from Ag⁺, which needs 1 electron per atom; so 2 F vs 1 F per mole.
items.markingKey: Cu²⁺ needs 2e⁻ [1]; Ag⁺ needs 1e⁻ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the mass of the anode decreases when copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed using copper electrodes.
items.answer: Copper atoms of the anode are oxidised to Cu²⁺ ions (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻), which go into solution.
items.markingKey: anode oxidised [1]; half-equation [1] [2]

items.stem: A current of 3 A is passed through aqueous silver nitrate for 15 minutes. What is the mass of silver deposited at the cathode? [F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹]
A current of 0.8 A is passed through molten sodium chloride for 10 minutes. Calculate the mass of sodium deposited at the cathode. [F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹]

A workshop in Kuala Lumpur electroplates a metal object of surface area 50 cm² with a layer of copper 25 μm thick, using a solution containing Cu²⁺ ions and a current of 2 A. The density of copper is 8.96 g cm⁻³. (a) State which electrode the object must be and write the half-equation for the reaction there. (b) Explain why the anode is often made of copper.
items.answer: (a) Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (b) The copper anode is oxidised to Cu²⁺ ions, replacing those removed from solution, so the concentration stays constant.
items.markingKey: (a) cathode [1]; half-equation [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: The copper anode is oxidised to Cu²⁺ ions; replacing those removed from solution; so the concentration stays constant (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Which expression links the Faraday constant, the Avogadro constant and the charge on an electron?
items.answer: F = Le
items.markingKey: Charge of one mole of electrons.

items.stem: Explain why the volume of oxygen produced in the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid is half the volume of hydrogen.
items.answer: Four electrons are released per O₂ formed but only two are needed per H₂; the same charge passes at each electrode so moles of O₂ = half moles of H₂.
items.markingKey: electrons per molecule [1]; same charge at each electrode [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Manila states: "One faraday deposits one mole of any metal." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: One faraday deposits one mole of a metal only if its ion has a 1+ charge; for M²⁺ it deposits 0.5 mol.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: One faraday deposits one mole of a metal only if its ion has a 1+ charge; for M²⁺ it deposits 0.5 mol. [2]

items.stem: A current of 1.5 A is passed through concentrated aqueous sodium chloride for 40 minutes. What is the volume of chlorine at room temperature and pressure (24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹) at the anode? [F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹]
items.answer: 448 cm³

items.stem: Kenji electrolysed copper(II) sulfate solution using copper electrodes and a constant current of 0.5 A for 50 minutes. The cathode gained 0.491 g. The charge on an electron is 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the number of electrons that passed through the circuit.

Leila electrolysed copper(II) sulfate solution using copper electrodes and a constant current of 0.2 A for 50 minutes. The cathode gained 0.193 g. The charge on an electron is 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. (a) Calculate the number of electrons that passed through the circuit. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.
Describe how you would determine a value for the Avogadro constant by electrolysis, and explain the calculation.
items.answer: Copper electrodes in CuSO₄(aq); clean, dry, weigh cathode; series circuit with ammeter and variable resistor; constant current for measured time; remove, wash with water then propanone, dry, reweigh; Q = It; mol Cu = Δm ÷ 63.5; mol e⁻ = 2 × mol Cu; number of electrons = Q ÷ e; L = number of electrons ÷ mol e⁻; sources of error.
items.markingKey: apparatus [1]; measurements [2]; Q = It [1]; mol e⁻ from mass [1]; L calculation [1]; error / improvement [1] [7]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "standard hydrogen electrode"?
options: An element in contact with a solution of its ions, or two ions of the same element in solution with an inert platinum electrode.
The potential difference between two half-cells under standard conditions, E°cell = E°(positive electrode) − E°(negative electrode).
A platinum electrode coated in platinum black, in contact with H₂ gas at 101 kPa and 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ ions at 298 K, assigned E° = 0.00 V.
A strip of filter paper soaked in saturated KNO₃(aq) that completes the circuit by allowing ions to move between half-cells without mixing the solutions.
items.answer: A platinum electrode coated in platinum black, in contact with H₂ gas at 101 kPa and 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ ions at 298 K, assigned E° = 0.00 V.
items.markingKey: Standard hydrogen electrode: a platinum electrode coated in platinum black, in contact with H₂ gas at 101 kPa and 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ ions at 298 K, assigned E° = 0.00 V.

items.stem: Explain why a salt bridge is needed in an electrochemical cell.
items.answer: It completes the circuit by allowing ions to flow between the half-cells, maintaining electrical neutrality, without allowing the solutions to mix.
items.markingKey: completes circuit / ion movement [1]; solutions do not mix [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain what the sign of a standard electrode potential shows about a half-cell.
items.answer: A more positive E° means the oxidised form is more easily reduced (better oxidising agent) relative to H⁺/H₂; a more negative E° means the reduced form is more easily oxidised (better reducing agent).
items.markingKey: positive: oxidised form easily reduced [1]; negative: reduced form easily oxidised [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell is made from the half-cells I₂(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻(aq) (E° = +0.54 V) and Sn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Sn(s) (E° = −0.14 V). Identify the positive electrode and state the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
items.answer: The I₂/2I⁻ half-cell is positive; electrons flow from the Sn²⁺/Sn half-cell to the I₂/2I⁻ half-cell.
items.markingKey: positive electrode [1]; direction [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell is made from the half-cells Cl₂(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Cl⁻(aq) (E° = +1.36 V) and Cr³⁺(aq) + 3e⁻ ⇌ Cr(s) (E° = −0.74 V). (a) Calculate the standard cell potential. (b) Identify the positive electrode and state the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
items.answer: (a) +2.10 V (b) The Cl₂/2Cl⁻ half-cell is positive; electrons flow from the Cr³⁺/Cr half-cell to the Cl₂/2Cl⁻ half-cell.
items.markingKey: (a) E°cell = E°(positive) − E°(negative) [1] = +1.36 − (−0.74) = +2.10 V [1] [2] (b) positive electrode [1]; direction [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell is made from the half-cells Fe²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Fe(s) (E° = −0.44 V) and Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg(s) (E° = −2.38 V). (a) Calculate the standard cell potential. (b) Identify the positive electrode and state the direction of electron flow in the external circuit.
items.answer: (a) +1.94 V (b) The Fe²⁺/Fe half-cell is positive; electrons flow from the Mg²⁺/Mg half-cell to the Fe²⁺/Fe half-cell.

items.stem: Ana measured the standard electrode potential of the Mg²⁺/Mg half-cell using a standard hydrogen electrode. The voltmeter read 2.38 V and the metal was the negative terminal. (a) Describe the standard hydrogen electrode. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction that happens in the metal half-cell when the cell delivers a current.
items.answer: (a) Platinum electrode coated with platinum black, dipping into 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺(aq) (e.g. HCl), with H₂ gas bubbled over it at 101 kPa, at 298 K. (b) Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: (a) Pt electrode [1]; 1.00 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ [1]; H₂ at 101 kPa, 298 K [1] [3] (b) Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ [1]

items.stem: Amara measured the standard electrode potential of the Pb²⁺/Pb half-cell using a standard hydrogen electrode. The voltmeter read 0.13 V and the metal was the negative terminal. (a) Explain why the concentration of the metal ion solution must be 1.00 mol dm⁻³. (b) Explain the function of the salt bridge and why it contains KNO₃. (c) Write the half-equation for the reaction that happens in the metal half-cell when the cell delivers a current.
items.answer: (a) The electrode potential depends on concentration (position of the equilibrium); standard values allow comparison. (b) Allows ions to move to complete the circuit without mixing the solutions; KNO₃ ions do not react with or precipitate the ions in the half-cells. (c) Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: (a) The electrode potential depends on concentration (position of the equilibrium) [1]; standard values allow comparison [1] [2] (b) function [1]; reason for KNO₃ [1] [2] (c) Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ [1]

items.stem: Explain why the standard hydrogen electrode is rarely used in practice and what is used instead.
items.answer: H₂ gas is flammable and difficult to keep at 101 kPa; platinum black is easily poisoned; a secondary standard (e.g. a calomel or Ag/AgCl reference electrode) of known E° is used.
items.markingKey: practical difficulties [1]; secondary reference electrode [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun says: "Electrons flow through the salt bridge." Explain whether Arjun is correct.
items.answer: Electrons flow through the external wire; ions move through the salt bridge.

items.answer: Cl₂

items.stem: Explain how E° values are used to decide whether a reaction is feasible.
items.answer: Identify the species reduced and oxidised; E°cell = E°(reduction half) − E°(oxidation half); if E°cell is positive the reaction is feasible.
items.markingKey: identify half-equations [1]; E°cell calculation [1]; positive → feasible [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why acidified potassium manganate(VII) can oxidise chloride ions but acidified potassium dichromate(VI) barely can.
items.answer: E°(MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺) = +1.52 V is more positive than E°(Cl₂/Cl⁻) = +1.36 V, so E°cell is +0.16 V; for dichromate +1.33 V is slightly less than +1.36 V, so E°cell is −0.03 V (not feasible under standard conditions).
items.markingKey: MnO₄⁻ comparison [1]; Cr₂O₇²⁻ comparison [1]; sign of E°cell [1] [3]

items.stem: Use the E° values Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Mg(s) E° = −2.38 V and Br₂(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Br⁻(aq) E° = +1.07 V. Will Mg²⁺ will react with Br⁻ under standard conditions?
options: It depends only on the masses used
items.answer: No; E°cell is negative

items.stem: Use the E° values Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s) E° = −0.76 V and Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s) E° = +0.34 V to predict whether Zn²⁺ will react with Cu under standard conditions. If a reaction occurs, write the equation.
items.answer: No: E°cell = −0.76 − (+0.34) = −1.10 V, negative; the reverse reaction is feasible instead.
items.markingKey: E°cell calculated [1]; correct conclusion [1]; reverse reaction identified [1] [3]

items.stem: Use the E° values Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Cu(s) E° = +0.34 V and Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ ⇌ Zn(s) E° = −0.76 V to predict whether Cu²⁺ will react with Zn under standard conditions. If a reaction occurs, write the equation.
items.answer: Yes: E°cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V, positive. Equation: Cu²⁺ + Zn → Cu + Zn²⁺.
items.markingKey: E°cell calculated [1]; correct conclusion [1]; balanced equation [1] [3]

items.stem: A student in Jakarta is given these data: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ ⇌ Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, E° = +1.52 V; Cl₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2Cl⁻, E° = +1.36 V; Fe³⁺ + e⁻ ⇌ Fe²⁺, E° = +0.77 V; I₂ + 2e⁻ ⇌ 2I⁻, E° = +0.54 V; Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ ⇌ 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, E° = +1.33 V. (a) Show that Fe³⁺ ions can oxidise iodide ions and write the equation. (b) Explain why the E° value of a half-cell containing H⁺ depends on pH.
items.answer: (a) E°cell = 0.77 − 0.54 = +0.23 V (positive); 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ (b) H⁺ appears in the half-equation; changing [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium and so changes the electrode potential (less positive at higher pH).
items.markingKey: (a) E°cell [1]; equation [1] [2] (b) H⁺ appears in the half-equation [1]; changing [H⁺] shifts the equilibrium and so changes the electrode potential (less positive at higher pH) [1] [2]
